title: Type Qualifiers & Specifiers
relevance: SDE interviews use this topic to test whether candidates understand compiler contracts—const-correctness, volatile for hardware/ISRs, and when restrict or _Atomic are required versus unsafe.

phases.goal: Establish that type qualifiers and specifiers are compiler contracts, not changes to how data is fundamentally represented in memory.

must_hit.point: Type qualifiers and specifiers are metadata on C declarations that change the contract with the compiler—what it may and must not do when optimizing—rather than typically changing how data is fundamentally represented in memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says they govern optimizer permissions/forbidden transformations, not the basic in-memory layout of the object.

must_hit.point: const declares that an object's value will not be modified after initialization and underpins const-correctness: functions advertise whether they modify data passed to them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions post-init immutability and API promises like strlen(const char *src) not writing through src.

must_hit.point: inline is a hint (not a command) to substitute a function body at the call site; register is a legacy register hint that modern compilers ignore for optimization but still forbids taking the address with &.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes hint vs command for inline, and notes & is illegal on register variables even if the optimizer ignores the hint.

probes: What do type qualifiers actually change for the compiler, if they usually do not change how an object is laid out in memory?
What does const promise about an object, and how does that show up in a function signature like strlen?

hints.1: Think about the agreement between you and the optimizer, not about sizeof or bit patterns.
hints.2: Start with const as a no-write-after-init promise, then how that promise appears on pointer parameters.
hints.3: Qualifiers/specifiers are metadata that constrain optimization; const means the value is not modified after initialization, enabling const-correct APIs.

phases.goal: Explain how const placement, volatile access rules, and restrict aliasing promises alter what the compiler may emit.

must_hit.point: The position of const relative to * changes meaning: const int *p / int const *p = pointer to constant data; int * const p = constant pointer to mutable data; const int * const p = constant pointer to constant data; int *p = both mutable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly classifies all four combinations using the right-left/declaration reading of where const sits vs *.

must_hit.point: volatile requires that every abstract-machine read and write to that object correspond to a physical read or write; the compiler must not cache values in registers, elide accesses, or reorder accesses to it when something outside the known flow of control may change it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says fresh memory accesses every time; cites MMIO, ISR-updated globals, or volatile sig_atomic_t in signal handlers.

must_hit.point: restrict (C99) promises that for the pointer's lifetime, if the object is modified, all accesses go only through that restrict pointer (or pointers derived from it)—an anti-aliasing optimization promise; overlapping memcpy buffers break it and yield undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the exclusive-access promise and that lying (e.g. overlapping memcpy) is UB / can corrupt via vectorized code.

must_hit.point: A global or static const is typically placed in a read-only segment (often .rodata in ELF); const and volatile can combine for a read-only hardware register the program must not write but must re-read because hardware updates it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions .rodata/read-only placement and gives const volatile for a status/timer-style MMIO register.

probes: Walk through the four const/pointer combinations and what each allows you to change.
What exactly does volatile force the compiler to do on each access, and when do you need it?
What promise does restrict make, and what goes wrong if two restrict pointers actually alias?

hints.1: Read declarations from the identifier: look at which side of * the const sits.
hints.2: Separate three ideas: const placement vs *; volatile = no cache/elide/reorder of those accesses; restrict = exclusive access for the optimizer.
hints.3: const int * vs int * const vs both; volatile maps each abstract access to a real one (MMIO/ISR/signals); restrict means only that pointer path may touch the object if it is modified—overlap with memcpy is UB.

phases.goal: Contrast optimization promises and concurrency tools: restrict vs non-restrict copies, and volatile visibility vs _Atomic atomicity.

must_hit.point: memcpy uses restrict and may use highly optimized vector instructions when dest and src do not overlap; memmove makes no restrict promise, remains safe for overlapping memory, but may be slower.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pairs non-overlap + speed (memcpy) against overlap-safe + potentially slower (memmove).

must_hit.point: volatile guarantees visibility by preventing compiler caching for hardware/ISRs but does not stop mid-update preemption; _Atomic (C11) guarantees atomicity and memory ordering for multi-threading so an operation completes entirely or not at all across cores.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Hardware/ISR → volatile; OS threads → _Atomic (or mutexes); does not treat volatile as thread sync.

must_hit.point: const volatile is the right combination when the CPU may only read a register that hardware can change at any time: volatile forces re-reads, const forbids program writes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains both roles on one pointer type for a read-only asynchronous hardware register.

probes: Why does the library offer both memcpy and memmove, and what does restrict have to do with it?
When would you choose volatile versus _Atomic for shared state?

hints.1: Ask whether the buffers can overlap, and whether the other writer is hardware/ISR or another thread.
hints.2: memcpy's restrict enables aggressive optimization; memmove stays correct on overlap. volatile is visibility to external agents; _Atomic is atomicity/ordering between threads.
hints.3: Non-overlapping copy → restrict/memcpy (faster, UB if you lie). Overlap → memmove. MMIO/ISR → volatile. Threads → _Atomic/mutexes, not volatile alone.

phases.goal: Apply qualifiers to polling loops, const-correct APIs, and memory-mapped registers.

must_hit.point: Without volatile on a hardware flag polled in a loop, the optimizer can hoist the read and turn the wait into an infinite loop; with volatile, each iteration emits a load so the loop ends when hardware sets the flag.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes hoist-to-if-then-while(1) without volatile versus per-iteration load with volatile.

must_hit.point: A const-correct finder like find_substring(const char *haystack, const char *needle) returning const char * advertises read-only inputs and stops the caller from modifying the haystack through the returned pointer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties const on parameters and return type to preventing accidental mutation of the source string.

must_hit.point: For an 8-bit memory-mapped receive register the CPU can read but not write, updated asynchronously by hardware, the pointer should be const volatile (as in the uart_rx example).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Fills in const volatile: const blocks C writes, volatile forces fresh reads of async hardware updates.

probes: What does volatile do, and is it enough to protect data shared between threads?
Why can a non-volatile polling loop on a hardware flag become an infinite loop under optimization?
How would you declare a pointer to a read-only memory-mapped UART receive register that hardware updates asynchronously?

hints.1: Consider what the optimizer assumes if nothing in the loop appears to write the flag.
hints.2: Contrast compiler-visible mutations with external agents (hardware, ISR); then ask about threads separately.
hints.3: volatile stops elision/caching of accesses for MMIO/ISRs but is not atomic and not a memory barrier—threads need mutexes or atomics; polling needs volatile; read-only MMIO needs const volatile.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: memcpy promises dest and src do not overlap via restrict, enabling aggressive optimization such as vectorized copies; memmove makes no such promise, so it is safe when regions overlap but may be slower.

Use volatile when communicating with hardware or an ISR so the compiler cannot cache or elide accesses (visibility to outside agents). Use _Atomic when communicating between OS threads so updates are atomic and ordered across cores. volatile alone is not thread synchronization.

tradeoffs.topic: const vs volatile on a hardware register
tradeoffs.strong_answer: const alone would allow caching of a value that hardware still changes; volatile alone would allow the program to write a read-only register. const volatile means the program must re-read every time and must not write.

gotchas.trap: Casting away const and modifying an object that was originally defined as const (e.g. a string literal or const global).
gotchas.correction: That is undefined behavior; the object may live in read-only memory and the OS may segfault on the write.

gotchas.trap: Using volatile for thread synchronization (the concurrency myth).
gotchas.correction: volatile is not atomic and not a memory barrier: it does not prevent data races or CPU reordering. Use _Atomic or mutexes for threads; reserve volatile for MMIO, ISRs, and related cases.

gotchas.trap: Passing overlapping buffers to memcpy after promising restrict.
gotchas.correction: Breaking the restrict promise is undefined behavior; the compiler may vectorize assuming no overlap and corrupt data. Use memmove when overlap is possible.

gotchas.trap: Polling a non-volatile hardware flag in a tight loop.
gotchas.correction: The optimizer may assume the value never changes inside the loop, hoist the read, and emit an infinite loop. Mark the object volatile so each iteration performs a real load.
